item.description: Just as they are expected to be ‘ideal’ immigrants in their adopted countries, the diaspora must also be unquestioning and uncritical of India.
item.content:encoded:
Since taking office in 2014, Prime Minister Narendra Modi has waged an energetic campaign to gain the support of the roughly five million Indian Americans. He has, in several speeches, urged the community to contribute money and expertise to his programmes in India. He has been keen to leverage the Indian diaspora to build political clout for himself in the US and increase monetary remittances to India.

The Indian diaspora is not homogenous and not so easy to unify. It comprises many religious, caste, linguistic and class groups. However, Modi recognised that many in these diverse groups are bound together by a powerful – but often elusive – sense of belonging and a connection to their motherland.

He shrewdly appealed to their shared love for India, tapping into a nostalgia for home and invoking a sense of pride in the land they had left behind. He tried to build coherence and unity by using this shared sense of identity as a foundation.

“The owner of this pattani (roasted green gram) shop doesn’t have an iota of mercy”, was my conclusion. Every year, the Vaikunta Ekadasi festival was held in Srirangam for 20 days. The crowds were humongous. Business was brisk in the shops. What profit could anyone earn from selling roasted green gram? I wouldn’t know. There were many kinds of measures: from tiny round padis of half a finger’s length and a finger’s width to pattanam padis with the volume of around a litre. Sale was made according to what the buyer could afford. The turnover was never more than a rupee. Most people bought roasted gram for copper coins and small change. item.title: As winter comes, a drought-hit district in Maharashtra fears the worst
item.description: From farmers and cattle breeders to sugar factories and migrant workers, no one is untouched by the crisis.
item.content:encoded:
Awasrao Powal, a 90-year-old, has seen many droughts rumble through Maharashtra’s Beed district. He vividly remembers the 1972 drought when farmers did not even sow seeds. “We had no food, but we still had water,” he recalled.

This year’s drought, he says, is worse. Most water sources have dried up in his village, Chumbali. “There is no money,” Powal said. “There is no work.”

Over two-thirds of Maharashtra – 304 out of 358 tehsils – have been declared drought-hit after the state recorded an 18% deficit in monsoon rains. In Beed, the deficit went up to 37%, making it the worst in a decade.

The drought is hurting farmers in every possible way.

Mustafa Khan’s cotton crop usually grows up to four feet to six feet, with 70 to 80 cotton pods. This year, the lack of rain has stunted it, reducing the number of cotton pods to less than 10.

“The crop has not matured,” he said. “The harvest is also not enough to feed my cattle.”

Khan has 12 cows, buffaloes and bulls. He said he has been buying fodder from the market, but prices have risen from Rs 10 per bundle to Rs 20 in the last two months.

item.title: From taboo subject, menopause is now a big business opportunity
item.description: Does it genuinely meet women’s needs, or does it help create a new market?
item.content:encoded:
Long relegated to the private sphere, Menopause is now the focus of unprecedented attention both in the media and commercially with a market value of 535 billion euros ($600 billion). The amount of books, podcasts, documentaries, digital applications, food supplements and coaching programs is multiplying to support women in this stage of life. What was once a taboo subject has become a booming economic sector.

This evolution constitutes an important step forward: people are talking more about menopause, it is better understood and is gradually being recognised as a public health issue. But this visibility is also accompanied by bold marketing. As the topic enters the public arena, it also becomes a niche market opportunity.

This transformation raises a question at the heart of the analysis in All Change! Marketing and Consuming the Menopause Transition: does it genuinely meet women’s needs, or does it help create a new market built on their concerns, symptoms and desire for wellbeing?

Commercialisation that shapes perceptions of menopause

The book conceptualises the emergence of menopause as a consumer market in its own right. This niche market is characterised by growing “climacteric market awareness” and by the gradual transformation of menopause into a space for commercial gain, bodily intervention and self-optimisation. On June 9, a “sudden and intense” carbon dioxide gas leak during a scheduled cylinder replacement at Schaeffler India’s Talegaon factory, killed two workers and affected three others, The Indian Express reported.

Schaeffler India manufactures automotive and industrial components, including bearings and precision machinery parts. It is the Indian subsidiary of the German Schaeffler Group.

The police had registered a case in July against six persons, including company officials and representatives of contractors involved in maintaining the factory’s fire-suppression system.

Kadam was taken into custody by the Talegaon MIDC Police Station under provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the company said on Tuesday.

item.title: Diet homogenisation is shrinking biodiversity: Why India must revive local vegetable varieties
item.description: Vegetable biodiversity is important for nutritional security and climate resilience. But it is rapidly declining.
item.content:encoded:
The clove bean is fondly known as mookuthi avarai in Tamil, an ode to its nose-pin-like appearance. Clove bean belongs to the same family as the morning glory, perennial fast-growing vines that are known for their brightly coloured flowers, and is not a true bean species.

Once a common vegetable in south Indian kitchens, clove bean now remains immortalised in S Meenakshi Ammal’s iconic cookbook Samaithu Paar (Cook and See in Tamil), first published in 1951.

Today, clove beans are a rare, if not an impossible sight in vegetable markets and seem to have completely disappeared from India’s culinary landscape. However, in one small farm in Bengaluru, landscape architect, natural farmer and founder of Hariyalee Seeds, Prabhakar Rao, continues to conserve the seeds of this and other long-forgotten vegetables.

As Rao walks around his farm’s undulating land, pointing to heirloom vegetables like the Yerengere white long eggplant or various tomato varieties, he laments how vegetable markets today are dominated by hybrids. There was a time when the Yerengere white long eggplant was the only brinjal variety that went into the making of vangi bath or brinjal rice, says Rao.

item.title: Fiction: Avdhi’s estranged mother’s death brings her back to Shimla, where the past awaits her
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Things We Carry Home’, by Savi Sharma.
item.content:encoded:
Shimla was still half-asleep when I arrived. The taxi climbed like someone trying to remember the end of a sentence. Mist sat in the hollows between trees; the world blurred into a soft, familiar grey. I watched the road and let my thoughts move slow; too slow to be useful, too steady to be denial.

I sat back, holding my bag, watching the city I once called home. It looked smaller somehow. Not physically, but in the way old classrooms do when you return as an adult. Like time had folded the place in half, and now it didn’t quite fit around me the same way.

When the taxi finally turned into our old lane, I felt it before I saw it, that quiet pull, like an ache waking up after too many years of sleep. The gate stood open, the paint peeling. It looked like any house that had nurtured a life inside it for years.

The State Bank of India on Wednesday said that a cyberattack had led to the leak of about 3.75 lakh customer records on the dark web, of which 3,897 contained personally identifiable information.

The leaked information included customers’ names, mobile numbers, dates of birth, gender, email addresses and residential addresses, the bank said in a filing to the stock exchanges.

The bank said the leak was not expected to have any impact on its operations or financial performance.

An independent cybersecurity agency has been engaged to conduct an assessment and investigate the nature and extent of the data leak, the bank added.

Digital rights organisation Internet Freedom Foundation flagged that the bank had not notified the customers whose data was leaked and had only informed the stock exchanges.

The organisation also said that the bank had learnt of the breach from external agencies after the data had been published online and did not yet know how the data had left its systems.

item.title: India rejects ‘negative’ portrayal at UN over ‘unverified’ human rights abuse allegations
item.description: A day earlier, the international organisation flagged the repeated ‘heavy-handed police response to demonstrations’, amid protests against CEC Gyanesh Kumar.
item.content:encoded:
India on Wednesday said that it opposed attempts to turn allegations of human rights abuses and “incomplete statistics” into a “negative characterisation” of the world’s largest democracy.

Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Ministry of External Affairs Deputy Secretary Barkha Tamrakar said that human rights should not be used as an instrument of political pressure or to selectively target countries.

The statement came a day after UN human rights experts flagged the repeated “heavy-handed police response to peaceful youth-led demonstrations” against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar for his handling of the special intensive revision of voter rolls.

The UN experts had noted that earlier this month, more than 7,000 persons, including journalists, human rights defenders, lawyers and political party members had been detained in New Delhi and taken to remote detention centres.

The experts described the crackdown as part of a “broader, troubling pattern”. They said that they had repeatedly alerted the Indian authorities about the “undue restrictions on peaceful assembly, excessive force, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances and the targeting of student activists”.

However, Tamrakar said on Wednesday that India was “anchored in the rule of law” and had signed the Convention on Enforced Disappearances.

item.title: A new book reconstructs the devastating Nam Ka Chu battle of the 1962 Sino-Indian War
item.description: An excerpt from ‘1962: Death Trap in Nam Ka Chu’, by Ashok Kalyan Verma with Shiv Kunal Verma.
item.content:encoded:
In the years leading up to 1962, the Himalaya, those quiet sentinels of snow and stone, became the stage for a clash of vision and will. On one side stood India still finding its feet in the first flush of independence, guided by faith in moral diplomacy. On the other, a China hardened by revolution, driven by clarity of purpose and the cold precision of long-term design.

While India spoke of Panchsheel, the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, Peking (now known as Beijing) built roads. In Tibet, the Chinese leadership knew exactly what needed to be done. Once their control was established by the end of 1951, they moved to consolidate the high plateau and turn it into a fortress, concentrating on the administrative, military, and psychological. The Khampa rebellions in eastern Tibet were ruthlessly suppressed. Roads began to snake across barren ridges, climbing higher each year, cutting deep into the silence of the mountains.

India watched but did not pay heed. In the comfort of diplomatic rhetoric, there was little realisation that a revolution in logistics and terrain control was underway on the other side of the frontier.

item.title: Bharatnatyam history: How stigmatised devadasis weathered social ostracism and moral outrage
item.description: An excerpt from ‘From The Corner of Her Eye: The Many Histories of Bharatanatyam’, by Justin McCarthy.
item.content:encoded:
The literacy of the dancing woman was aimed at acquiring a specific set of arts-related skills. Skills of elegant refinement, yes, but nevertheless skills suitable to feudal times and places. Wood’s famous “Despatch” of 1854 outlined the East India Company’s vision of literacy for a colonial India. When Sir Wood, the viscount of Halifax, called for female schooling, he certainly was not thinking of the “otherly” education of the dancing woman.

As early as the 1820s, even before Wood’s ultimately enduring plans for primary, secondary and collegiate instruction were implemented, precocious steps towards girls’ schools had been taken in the Madras Presidency. Such schools, though typified as secular, were destined for Christian and/or “caste” girls, i.e. Hindus from Brahmin, royal and merchant families. We can assume that the children of dancing women were not welcome, no matter how sophisticated their mothers may have been. Nor would many dancing women have entertained the idea of sending their offspring to such schools. item.title: When mangrove restoration projects become big business
item.description: It has become a new kind of market. But it also distributes what it generates along a chain of intermediaries, with little reaching local communities.
item.content:encoded:
On Pakistan’s Indus delta coast, a 350,000-hectare mangrove project is turning a growing forest into something that can be sold to companies thousands of miles away: carbon credits.

Carbon credits allow companies to pay for projects that store carbon or prevent further emissions, with each credit equalling a certain amount of carbon. Restoring mangroves can generate credits as a healthy, growing forest absorbs and stores carbon. It’s part of a thriving billion dollar industry.

But that forest was already worth something to the thousands of people living there. It protects 60 villages from storms, provides nursery habitat for fish and is a source of wood, honey and thatch.

The difference points to a bigger problem. A mangrove has at least two kinds of value: the value that can be packaged and sold to a (wealthy) distant buyer, and the value that is experienced locally but is much harder to monetise. Only the first has a market built around it.

This gap will be under the spotlight at the upcoming UN climate summit Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, this November. At last year’s Cop30, governments called for the money provided by wealthy countries to help communities cope with the consequences of climate change to at least triple by 2035. item.description: An excerpt from ‘O’ Beloved, The Heart Sings’, by Madhu Kailas.

Every night I starve and pine,
Looking at the moon and its light.
I hear from the wayfarers who have seen her,
That my beloved is more beautiful than the moon.


Because I have nothing to offer her,
Because I do not know how to reach her heart,
My heart loves her with the last drop of blood
Just to keep itself alive.


Amid an ominous, murderous thunderstorm
I could only see my beloved’s face
Reflected in piercing flashes of lightning strikes,
Ripping apart my anguished heart.


After the rains we stepped out of the shelter,
The scent of wet earth consumed us.
I touched my beloved’s hand gently like a feather,
The beads of water had turned to pearls on her form.


One more sunset, the birds are returning home.

item.title: India at growing risk of infectious diseases due to climate change effects
item.description: Excess rainfall allows bacteria and viruses to thrive and spread while drought-like conditions can intensify transmission and hygiene dangers.
item.content:encoded:
When extreme weather events occur, the damage is usually measured in collapsed buildings, damaged roads and flooded homes. But the aftermath also brings a less visible threat.

Heatwaves, droughts, erratic rainfall and flash floods, in combination or alone, also reshape the ecology of diseases. They can affect how long pathogens survive, change the distribution of disease-carrying insects and bring people, animals and pathogens into closer contact, increasing the risk of outbreaks in new places at unexpected times.

The latest assessment report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has warned that heatwaves and extreme rainfall events are projected to increase in the coming years.

A 2025 study by IPE Global, an international development consultancy, and Esri India, a GIS mapping company, warns that extreme weather could become more severe by 2030, with heatwaves projected to double in major cities and extreme rainfall events expected to rise by 43% across the country.

Health experts state that we need to factor in and prevent climate-related outbreaks rather than simply responding to them.

The first horse rides in through our screens. item.title: ‘The Future Is Peace’: A Palestinian‑Israeli memoir seeks to break the cycle of violence
item.description: The memoir stands out as a rare work of true, focused resolution, which highlights the shared humanity at the heart of an intractable conflict.
item.content:encoded:
Since the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023, the world has witnessed unimaginable, almost constant violence in Gaza and the West Bank. But people’s understanding of these events is not universal – each person is exposed to a particular set of narratives surrounding history, victimhood and trauma.

The vast majority of news reports, social media posts, videos, and books that have covered the events since October 7, 2023 can be defined as what I call “conflict media”, which reproduces the divisions of the conflict it describes, perpetuating it to the point where the media itself becomes a weapon in an information war.

As a scholar of the Middle East, I have rarely – though not never – encountered conflict media’s opposite, which I call “resolution media”.

The most famous works of resolution media have emerged after a conflict ends, and highlight the universal suffering of war. item.title: India and Pakistan have forgotten the most enduring lesson of the Cuban missile crisis
item.description: After the dangerous escalation in May 2025, the world cannot afford another confrontation in Southasia which tests assumptions that fortuitously survived once.
item.content:encoded:
At the height of the Cuban missile crisis, American warships dropped small explosive charges near a Soviet submarine off the coast of Cuba on October 27, 1962. Their purpose was to force the B-59 submarine to surface. The Americans did not know that it carried a nuclear torpedo. Inside the submarine, officers who had been cut off from reliable communications struggled to determine whether war had begun.

Captain Valentin Savitsky came close to ordering the torpedo’s use but another senior officer aboard, Vasili Arkhipov, helped prevent that decision. The episode was fully understood decades later, a reminder of how close the world came to the use of nuclear weapons through misperception, incomplete information, and compressed decision timelines under stress.

The incident, dramatised in The Man Who Saved the World, a 2012 television documentary in the PBS series Secrets of the Dead series, illustrates how nuclear escalation can begin without either belligerent choosing to go nuclear. One side conducts an operation it considers limited while the other encounters explosions, incomplete information and uncertainty about what will happen next. Decisions then depend on officers under tremendous pressure, interpreting intentions they cannot verify.

The 88-hour long military conflict between India and Pakistan in May 2025 brought this problem into sharper focus,...

item.title: Sunday book pick: In ‘Agostino’, an adolescent boy is forced to see his mother as a woman
item.description: Alberto Moravia’s novella was first published in Italian in 1945. Michael F Moore’s translation came out in 2014.
item.content:encoded:
He repeated to himself “She’s only a woman” with the objective indifference of a connoisseur. But one moment later, unable to bear his mother’s unawareness or his own attentions, he wanted to shout, “Cover yourself, stop showing yourself to me, I’m not who I used to be.”

Italian writer Alberto Moravia’s novella, Agostino, published in 1945, is about a summer holiday which starts pleasantly but is soured by the “loss” of a young boy’s innocence.

Thirteen-year-old Agostino and his widowed mother are visiting the beach for the summer. Agostino is in awe of his mother – who is repeatedly described as big and beautiful – and is proud to enjoy her undivided attention. He feels the eyes on them, imagining them performing their parts for the world. He is hypnotised by her capaciousness and the ease with which she swims, plays, and protects him. His affection for her is magnetic, bordering on “infatuation”, which the narrator acknowledges as a special kind of “turmoil.”

item.title: A journey within: Reflections on translating Lithuanian writer Jaroslavas Melnikas into Hindi
item.description: ‘The Last Day’ is the first Lithuanian book to be translated into any Indian language. It has been translated into Hindi by Rekha Sethi as ‘Antim Din.’
item.content:encoded:
Lithuanian writer Jaroslavas Melnikas writes from the edge of certainty. His fictional world is one where reality constantly slips into another, where ordinary lives suddenly confront metaphysical doubt, and where human beings stand suspended between the visible and the invisible. I was drawn to this unsettling world long before I began translating The Last Day into Hindi. These stories not only captivated my literary sensibility but also led me toward self-reflection.

The paradoxes and predicaments faced by the characters in this collection were deeply rooted in human consciousness. Melnikas’ characters inhabit unstable realities where everyday life suddenly fractures, exposing loneliness, moral ambiguity, and the fragility of certainty. There was something profoundly familiar in his exploration of existence, freedom, memory, and identity, as though his stories were speaking to anxieties already embedded within me.

Lithuanian, one of the oldest surviving European languages, remains relatively unfamiliar in the Indian literary sphere. Melnikas himself occupies a compelling cultural position. Born in western Ukraine and living in Lithuania for the past three decades, he writes in both Ukrainian and Lithuanian, though in recent years Lithuanian has become his primary literary language. item.title: The kitchen came first, then god: Five recipes from an emerging Jewish community in Andhra Pradesh
item.description: Exploring the kitchens of the Bene Ephraim.
item.content:encoded:
When Ravi Shemesh’s uncle died recently, the family cooked pappu charu.

It is a sour lentil broth, made frequently in nearly every household in coastal Andhra Pradesh.

The Shemesh family made it in a large pot on the fire in the yard, on a mud and brick stove, wood underneath. It was served to all the relatives after the funeral.

There was another kitchen in the house, indoors, with fitted cupboards and a granite worktop and a gas hob, and that was where Ravi’s mother rolls and griddles the chapatis. But the big pots go outside, on the fire.

Which is why, when they cook meat, the neighbours catch the smell. They' are usually given a little.

The house is in Yerajerla, a village near Ongole in Prakasam district, where ten Jewish families live. It was Ravi’s father’s place. And it’s a community. A very small one, but a community nevertheless.

Ravi’s mother is Sippora but at home she is called Chittemma. She was born up the coast in Kotha Reddy Palem, in the house of her grandfather Yacob Yacobi. She married into this village.

item.title: ‘A writer too faithful to history is not a fiction writer’: Novelist MG Vassanji

The two-time Giller Prize-winning Canadian-Indian author MG Vassanji’s latest novel, The Apparition, is a textured story set during a tumultuous time in the history of the Delhi Sultanate at the cusp of sociopolitical change. Alauddin Khalji is the Sultan of Delhi, but lately, due to intoxication and poor health, it appears he no longer has a grip on the throne. His subjects speculate about how long he’ll hold on to it, though he still terrorises them. item.title: Ramachandra Guha: India’s classical music unites faiths. Its syncretic heritage must be preserved
item.description: More than any other field, it is classical music where Hindus and Muslims have lived, worked, laboured and created together.
item.content:encoded:
Some 20 years ago, I was in Lahore for an academic conference, where I met an aspiring classical vocalist who travelled every week to learn from a teacher in Karachi. Though I cannot hold a note myself, I have had a lifelong love for Hindustani music. I was thus surprised to learn from this talented Pakistani singer that his teacher spoke derisively of a particular raga as one that “belonged to the Hindus” (woh toh Hinduon ka raga hai).

I didn’t have the heart to tell the young man that such distinctions did not exist among classical musicians in India, or that a singer he admired, Roshanara Begum, had continued to sing the ragas, Shankara and Durga, after she moved to Pakistan even though they were named for Hindu deities. I could also have mentioned Salamat Ali Khan’s rendition of Nadiya Kinare Mora Gaon where this singer (who also lived in Pakistan) explains that the thumri is based on the love of Radha for Krishna.

Admittedly, both Roshanara and Salamat were born well before Partition when such seamless interchange of ideas and motifs between different faiths was part of the musical culture of undivided India.

item.title: Data shows 73% decline in world’s wildlife population – and more animals are not being counted
item.description: The numbers gathered by the Living Planet Index numbers, which are the most comprehensive available, are still far from complete.
item.content:encoded:
Wildlife populations around the world have declined by an average of 73% since 1970. That’s according to the WWF’s new 2026 Living Planet Index – a major estimate, updated every two years, of the changing state of nature. This does not mean that 73% of the world’s animals have disappeared. Rather, it is the average decline in the size of wildlife populations that is being monitored.

The index is one of the metrics used to track progress towards the UN’s biodiversity goals and shapes narratives of biodiversity loss across the world. But the data behind that 73% headline, one of the most comprehensive available, is still far from complete.

Very few, outside of those of us working at the coalface of handling biodiversity data, understand just how poorly wild animal populations are monitored. Though the world faces the joint crises of climate change and biodiversity loss, we can track climate change through thousands of weather stations or measures of atmospheric CO₂. Biodiversity is far harder to measure. Counting wildlife is highly resource intensive, generally can’t be done from space, and systematic monitoring is extremely patchy.

“Twenty years ago, all this was paddy,” says Nazir Ahmad, a farmer from Qaimoh, a village in south Kashmir’s Kulgam district, pointing at the rows of apple saplings that now cover his land. Today, much of that landscape has changed. The irrigation channels set up for paddy still exist, running through the fields as they always have. However, the paddy they once fed has given way to apple plantations.

Across Kashmir, farmers are increasingly replacing food crops with horticulture, especially apple orchards, as they seek higher returns amid rising cultivation costs.

For many growers, the calculation is straightforward. Paddy offers modest returns, while apples, particularly high-density plantations, promise significantly higher earnings. item.title: Internet access a fundamental right for all, including children, says SC
item.description: ‘To deny the same altogether would be as absurd as saying children below a certain age do not have a freedom of speech worth expressing,’ said the bench.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court has said that every citizen, including children, has a fundamental right to use the internet.

“To deny the same altogether would be as absurd as saying children below a certain age do not have a conscience worth protecting or a freedom of speech worth expressing,” said a bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran in an order passed on Thursday.

The bench was hearing a petition alleging that social media platforms were failing to meet their legal obligations to report child sexual exploitation and abuse material to the authorities.

In its judgement, the court deliberated whether children should be completely shielded from the internet and social media platforms.

However, it pointed out that children's safety and freedom were not at odds. “Our children are entitled to both,” the court noted.

The observations came months after the BBC reported that it had found that social media platform Instagram, which is owned by Meta, had been running paid advertisements that promote child sexual abuse material in India.

Publishing or transmitting child sexual abuse material is illegal and constitutes a serious criminal offence under the 2000 Information Technology Act and the 2012 Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act.

item.title: ‘I wrote a children’s book about an insult I faced. Later, I had the same thought about my daughter’
item.description: Tamil American novelist and essayist Lakshmi Iyer on ‘colourism’.
item.content:encoded:
I typed the word and stopped. Kaali. Two syllables, said by a grandmother to a 12-year-old, in a book meant for readers who are ten. The cursor blinked after the i. Outside, the school bus trundled past our home. I was relieved to get away from my manuscript to make coffee for the kids. Excavating memories is never fun.

Kaali. Black one. Dark one. Is it a slur? Kaali is an adjective, a nickname. It masquerades as concern. It comes from the people who love you, over breakfast, with a palm against your cheek.

‘Even though she is dark, she glows’

I know this because I was that child. Sixth grade, maybe seventh, and Amma is mixing kadalai maavu with paal yedu and a pinch of manjal podi, spreading the creamy paste across my face, waiting for it to dry to a crust before washing it off. I quite enjoyed the ritual, the feeling of amma’s soft palms against my cheek, the chill of the paste evaporating from the heat of my skin, the film tightening the skin until it stretched and you could no longer smile or speak. I used to stand in front of the mirror, my turmeric-tinged face staring back at me like a mask....

item.title: How photography helped physicist Bibha Chowdhuri see the invisible in the 1930s
item.description: The scientist used light-sensitive plates to trace cosmic particles, contributing to pioneering research in particle physics.
item.content:encoded:
In 1939, a 26-year-old physicist published an article that contains what, at first, reads like instructions for an eccentric treasure hunt: place photographic plates in a refrigerator in Calcutta, in Darjeeling or in a Dak Bungalow at Sandakphu. But Bibha Chowdhuri was not looking for buried treasure. She was looking for traces of the invisible.

The plates had been prepared with samarium sulphate and exposed for months to cosmic radiation. When two of those placed at Sandakphu were developed, they revealed 30 “star-like tracks” – microscopic records of nuclear disintegration. The photographs transformed an otherwise invisible encounter between cosmic rays and matter into something that could be seen and studied.

Chowdhuri’s experiment belonged to a new kind of scientific image-making, pioneered in part by physicist Marietta Blau, in which photographic emulsions became detectors of subatomic events. Working with DM Bose at Calcutta’s Bose Institute, Chowdhuri would go on to develop methods for distinguishing particles by the tracks they left in photographic plates. Her work formed part of a chain of experiments that culminated in Cecil Powell’s Nobel Prize-winning research on mesotrons.

In the history books, Tenzing Norgay is hyphenated with the New Zealand mountaineer Edmund Hillary when discussing their feat of becoming the first men to have successfully scaled the world’s highest peak. Right from a young age, Norgay is desperate to climb the mountain that he worships. The world calls it Mount Everest, after a British surveyor. item.title: In pictures: Art and dissent by Bengal’s outspoken Durga Puja pandals in a changed political climate
item.description: Some pandals have embraced overtly religious and nationalist narratives while others have tried to be subversive, though not openly.
item.content:encoded:
Last year, around the time of Durga Puja, public anxiety in West Bengal was mounting with reports of Bengali-speaking people being expelled across the border after being accused of being Bangladeshi.

There was nervousness about citizenship rights and the right to vote due to the approaching Special Intensive Revision of the electoral rolls.

In response, Durga Puja pandals erected for the state’s most popular festival became powerful vehicles for asserting Bengali identity.

For instance, the theme at the Chaltabagan Sarbojanin pandal in Kolkata was “Ami Banglay Bolchi”, I Am Speaking Bengali. It traced the history of the Bengali language. The Aswininagar Bandhumahal pandal explored the historical journeys of Bengalis through changing political and riverine landscapes. The pandal of the Ramgarh Raipur Club told the stories of migrant workers who could not return home for the festival.

These were artistic interventions confronting exclusion in a political climate in which language and identity had become grounds for suspicion.

item.title: ‘How to Date a Fanatic’: Aruni Kashyap’s new novel is hopeful of getting a more tolerant India
item.description: The characters, who mostly belong to the North East and have lived through violence, seem to know better than many how to negotiate a conflict-ridden India.
item.content:encoded:
While reading Aruni Kashyap’s second novel, How to Date a Fanatic, I was confronted with a curious and delicious problem – how does one slot this novel and the novelist? When Kashyap debuted with A House with a Thousand Stories in 2013, a coming-of-age story about young Pablo set against the backdrop of insurgency, the novel could firmly be located in Mayong, Kashyap’s hometown in Assam, and in the tradition of Assamese novelists writing in English.

With the publication of his collection of short stories, His Father’s Disease, in 2019, one noted an expansion, both in terms of the geographical location that extended from Assam to Minnesota and its thematic preoccupation with violence, both personal and political, that stretched to explore issues of identity, sexuality, racism and belonging.

But with his latest novel, Kashyap seems to have shattered barriers of regionalism and set expectations for the writer belonging to the North East, the stranglehold of both of which he had scathingly critiqued in his short story “Skylark Girl,” to write a novel that compels you to place his writing on a wider, even planetary map.

item.title: Trump puts on hold law allowing 100% tariffs on India, four others for buying Russian oil
item.description: The United States president said that waiving the sanctions, which were to take effect on Sunday, was in the interest of the US.
item.content:encoded:
United States President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order putting on hold a law that allows him to impose tariffs of up to 100% on India and other countries that purchase Russian oil and gas.

Trump told the US Congress that the waiver was in the interest of the US.

While Trump had given his assent to the legislation on September 18, the signing of the bill into law had not automatically triggered the tariffs.

The law states that the tariffs could apply to the five countries that imported the largest volumes of Russian crude oil or natural gas in the 12 months before the law takes effect, if they knowingly continue buying Russian crude oil 30 days after the law is enacted.

The president’s order pausing the implementation of the law comes before the 30-day period was to conclude on Sunday.

Trump’s decision also came a week after he announced that the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to lower global energy prices. This was despite such a purchase potentially hurting its partner Ukraine in its war with Russia.

item.title: ‘A line moves people’: Cartoonist Amruta Patil on the graphic narrative exhibition she has curated
item.description: ‘The evolution of graphic storytelling tradition in India is the evolution of our nation,’ she added. ‘A Moving Line’ is on display at MAP, Bengaluru.
item.content:encoded:
Comics have been making their way into museums and art galleries for a while now. Over the last couple of years alone, Kolkata mounted an exhibition on the material craft of comics on the heels of a historical survey of Bengali comics from the 1920s to the present. Delhi’s Kiran Nadar Museum of Art turned itself into an embodied romp across the history of comics, inexplicably buffeted on both sides by a live archive of zines. All this alongside the Comic Cons trudging along each year while the Indie Comix Fests undyingly hop across cities as an open-source, comics-focused alternative.

Cartoonist Amruta Patil’s new exhibition A Moving Line, which opened at MAP Bengaluru on July 24, brings together more than 250 works spanning artefacts across millennia: temple carvings from Bengaluru’s own Someshwara temple to kaavad shrines and pattachitra scrolls; from the Tagore family’s early experiments with social caricature and the Ray family’s patronage for Sandesh to Amar Chitra Katha and Tinkle; from the deflatingly satirical strips of Bengal’s Basantak to glimpses of Pran’s Chacha Chaudhary and Falah Faisal’s Musalman; from thousands of webcomics blooming across platforms to the ongoing boom in graphic novels. It presents, as Patil herself put it, a constellation of idea clusters rather than an exhaustive chronology.

item.title: In France, student protests are driven by real concerns but are also a rite of passage
item.description: For many people school demonstrations are a key part of the formation of their role as citizen-protestors.
item.content:encoded:
Across France, school students have taken to the streets to protest about teacher shortages, dilapidated school buildings and long school days.

While the tradition of student protest has long roots in France, the country’s current fiscal crisis combined with entrenched structural problems with teacher recruitment, sickness absence and a backlog of school maintenance means this is unlikely to be something the current government can easily address.

Problems – and protests – regarding conditions in French schools go back decades.

I’ve spent 20 years conducting research in France and protest has been a recurring theme. Many research participants I’ve worked with have spoken with fondness about protesting as high school students.

One participant in Nanterre, who went on to become a community activist, repeatedly spoke about how schools in poor Paris suburbs were institutions that would “crush you”. This was due in part to French educational culture, but also because of their under-resourcing and poor state of repair. To them protest felt like an outlet for these grievances.

item.title: India’s per capita GDP below Bangladesh in 2026: IMF
item.description: The per capita gross domestic product of Bangladesh at current prices is $2,886 against India’s $2,749, the global financial body said.
item.content:encoded:
The International Monetary Fund has said that Bangladesh’s per capita gross domestic product is higher than that of India in 2026.

The per capita gross domestic product of Bangladesh at current prices is $2,886 against India’s $2,749, according to long-term data and forecasts in IMF’s latest World Economic Outlook published on October 13.

Per capita gross domestic product is a measure of a country’s economic output per person. It is calculated by dividing the country's gross domestic product by its population.

The average per capita gross domestic product in emerging markets and developing economies is about $7,746. The global average is about $15,889.

In 2027, Bangladesh’s per capita gross domestic product is estimated to be $3,219, ahead of India’s $3,036, the data showed. Bangladesh will maintain the marginal lead in 2028.

However, in 2029, India’s per capita gross domestic product of $3,661 will top Bangladesh’s $3,334, according to the International Monetary Fund.

A previous version of the report published on April 14 said that the per capita gross domestic product of Bangladesh at current prices at the time was $2,911 against India’s $2,812.
